  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`

  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a

  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging` (`mod.rs`)

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/mod.rs::invlpg` — the body is a single
  `core::arch::asm!` block issuing the `invlpg` instruction, which flushes the CPU TLB
  entry for `vaddr`. Verus does not support inline-asm expressions, so the body cannot be
  verified — an external-bottom hardware trust boundary (same class as the volatile
  page-table access in `table::read`/`write` and the int-to-pointer materialization in
  `frame::instance`/`bump_allocator::alloc`). See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-mod/verus-unsupported.md`. The effect is purely on hardware TLB
  state (outside Verus' memory model and invisible to every caller's Rust-visible state),
  so the faithful contract is **empty**: no `requires` (any `usize` is accepted), trivial
  `ensures` (returns `()`, no Rust-visible effect, every caller-side invariant preserved).
  This matches the inherited upstream
  `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs:151`
  `pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::paging::invlpg ](vaddr: usize);` (no
  `requires`/`ensures`). No exec signature changed.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `mm::phys`

  mandatory `external_body`) registering the foreign `alloc::collections::LinkedList<T, A>` as a

  downstream crate from implementing vstd's `View` / `ForLoopGhostIterator` for the foreign type,

  every frame in `phys_regions_frame_set(&physical_memory_regions)` becomes reserved.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same `LinkedList` limitation.
  `ensures` states that, on `Ok`, every *covered* frame in `mmio_regions_frame_set(mmio_regions)`
  becomes reserved (uncovered MMIO frames are skipped, matching the `frame::is_covered` gate).

the same wording class as the `frame.rs` singleton wrappers (`frame::alloc` … "external_body

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::Upool` (struct) — **ELIMINATED** (no longer `external_body`).
  The type is now machine-verified (`#[verus_verify]`). It is never constructed in verified code

1. ---
2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36. 
37. Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.
39. 
40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52. 
53. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
54. 
55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
56. 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
58. 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
63.    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
64.    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.
65. 
66. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
67. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
68. verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
69. rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.
70. 
71. **Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
74. copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.
75. 
76. - **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
77. - **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
78.   derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
79.   the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
80.   `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
81.   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
82.   in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
83. - **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.
87. 
88. **Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
90. on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
91. vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
92. used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
93. `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
94. state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),

name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.

# Spec Design Guide

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.

   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions

   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or

   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
   prevents accidentally omitting one arm:

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures
       result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
   ```
   Good:
   ```
   ensures match result {
       Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
       Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
   }
   ```
8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
   already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
   derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
   delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
   reviews harder.
10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
   Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
    every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
    invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.
12. **`uninterp` as Verification Escape** — using `uninterp spec fn` to
    avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
    via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
    `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function
    whose behavior is entirely under our control.
    `uninterp spec fn` is banned. All spec functions must have concrete
    definitions. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()` of an
    `external_body` type, that is a mechanical consequence of the type
    being `external_body` — the trust obligation is tracked there, not
    as a separate `uninterp` allowance. If a spec function is hard to
    define concretely, that is a signal to simplify the abstraction,
    not to use `uninterp`.

### Error Path Spec Principles

Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
   predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
   code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
   impossible?
3. **Liveness** — if the preconditions and current state make success
   possible, the spec must guarantee success (i.e., the function must
   not spuriously return `None`/`Err`). A spec that *allows* failure
   even when success is achievable is under-specified — callers cannot
   rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:
   ```
   ensures match result {
       Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
       Err(e) => /* error postcondition */,
   }
   ```
   This makes both arms visible for review — neither path is silently omitted.

### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort

**Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
- **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
- **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

**Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
- **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
  `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
  warrant no further properties.
- **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
  verified function with no additional logic.

### Property Coverage Checklist

When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.

1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
   - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
   - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
   - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms

2. **Safety** — What must never happen?
   - Bounds, disjointness, uniqueness, conservation, injectivity, ordering, monotonicity

3. **Liveness** — What good things must happen?
   - Guaranteed success conditions, resource availability, recoverability

4. **Structural Consistency** — Is the data self-consistent?
   - Type invariants, field relationships, valid ranges

### Invariant Design

Two kinds of invariants appear during specification:

- **Type invariant (`inv()`)** — defined on the View type (see **view-design**
  skill). Every constructor must establish it; every method must preserve it.
  If a property appears in `requires` of nearly every method, it belongs in
  `inv()` instead.
- **Loop invariant** — defined on loops. Must hold on entry (base case),
  be preserved by each iteration (inductive step), and together with the
  exit condition imply the function's `ensures` (sufficiency). Define
  complex invariants as `spec fn` predicates rather than inline clauses.

Both should reference View fields and abstract state, not implementation
details.

### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement

**Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
verification?

**Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
(e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.

**No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
`// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
verification work knows to clean it up.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their

dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A

verification work knows to clean it up.

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
for reference.

See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for the complete step-by-step guide
on View design, invariants, and method specifications.

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
   swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
   `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
   abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).
5. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
   Put reusable spec helpers on the View type instead.

For full View design methodology, see the **view-design** skill.

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust
impl FooView {
    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
    }
}
// ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
```

**Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
verification?

**Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
(e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.

**No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
`// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
verification work knows to clean it up.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

---

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
**The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
`external_body`, and `axiom`. Which functions belong in this category
is pre-determined by the TCB allowed list — do not make new trust
boundary decisions during specification or proving.

### Rules

- The caller analysis and View design identify external-top properties.
- Trust boundary decisions (which functions get `external_body`) are
  pre-approved in the TCB allowed list. Do not classify new functions
  as trust boundaries — if a function is not in the list, it must be
  fully verified.
- When writing `assume_specification`, follow the audit checklist in
  Part 1 (Anti-Patterns, Verification Escape).

---

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
for reference.

See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for the complete step-by-step guide
on View design, invariants, and method specifications.

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
   swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
   `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
   abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).
5. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
   Put reusable spec helpers on the View type instead.

For full View design methodology, see the **view-design** skill.

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust
impl FooView {
    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
    }
}
// ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
```

2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-manager/find_callers_output.md`
5. (generated by `scripts/find_callers_lsp.py`, rust-analyzer LSP, intra-crate).
6. 
7. ## Module Summary
8. 
9. | Category | Count |
10. |----------|------:|
11. | Total exec functions | 7 |
12. | Public / `pub(super)` | 6 |
13. | Private | 1 (`check_user_watermark`) |
14. | Types | 1 (`PhysMemoryManager`) |
15. 
16. All callers are inside the `kernel` crate. No external crate depends on this
17. module, so the entire caller set is the table below.
18. 
19. ## Verification-order Target Functions — call sites
20. 
21. | Function | Visibility | External callers | Where |
22. |----------|-----------|-----------------:|-------|
23. | `init` | `pub(super)` | 1 | `mm/phys/mod.rs:189` (subsystem `init`) |
24. | `alloc_kernel_frame` | `pub` | 4 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:217, 267, 600, 705` |
25. | `alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:748` (`alloc_kpages`) |
26. | `alloc_many_user_frames` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:611` (`alloc_upages`) |
27. | `alloc_user_frame` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/vmem.rs:879` (CoW fault resolve) |
28. | `check_user_watermark` | private | 0 external | called by `alloc_many_user_frames` (L177) and `alloc_user_frame` (L205) |
29. 
30. Supporting (not a target, but every alloc reaches the manager through it):
31. `get_mut` (`pub unsafe`) — 7 call sites. Every caller obtains the singleton via
32. `unsafe { PhysMemoryManager::get_mut() }.<alloc>()`, justified by the kernel being
33. single-threaded with interrupts disabled.
34. 
35. ## Trait Obligations
36. None. `PhysMemoryManager` implements no traits relevant to dispatch
37. (`Drop`/`GlobalAlloc`/`Iterator` etc.). All usage is direct method calls on the
38. singleton. The frame ownership wrappers it returns (`KernelFrame`, `UserFrame`)
39. *do* carry `Drop` semantics (dropping frees the frame), and callers depend on
40. that — see below.
41. 
42. ## Internal Call Graph
43. - `alloc_many_user_frames` → `check_user_watermark(count)` → `frame::free_count`,
44.   `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK`, then `self.upool.alloc()` per frame.
45. - `alloc_user_frame` → `check_user_watermark(1)` → `self.upool.alloc()`.
46. - `alloc_kernel_frame` → `frame::alloc` → `KernelFrame::new` (frees the frame on
47.   wrap failure).
48. - `alloc_many_kernel_frames` → `frame::alloc_contiguous(count)` →
49.   `KernelFrame::new` per frame (frees the leftover contiguous range on failure).
50. 
51. Key structural fact for the View: **user** allocations flow through `Upool`
52. (`self.upool`) and are watermark-gated; **kernel** allocations go straight to the
53. `frame` allocator and bypass the watermark.
54. 
55. ## Caller Expectations
56. 
57. ### `init(upool) -> Result<(), Error>`
58. Single caller: `mm/phys/mod.rs::init`, exactly once during single-threaded boot,
59. immediately after `Upool::new()`. Followed by `proof!{ lemma_manager_ready(); }`.
60. - Callers assume (Ok): the manager singleton now exists and holds the provided
61.   `upool`; subsequent `get_mut()` will not panic; the subsystem reaches the
62.   `manager_ready` / `live()` state. This is the post-state the surrounding
63.   `phys::init` spec advertises (`phys_view().live()`).
64. - Callers assume (Err): only `InvalidArgument`, and only on double-init; boot
65.   treats this as fatal (propagated with `?`).
66. - Callers don't care about: the `MaybeUninit` storage, the `AtomicBool` init
67.   flag, or the atomic ordering. They care only that "after Ok, the manager is
68.   ready and frame guarantees become meaningful."
69. 
70. ### `alloc_kernel_frame(&mut self) -> Result<KernelFrame, Error>`
71. Callers: `new_vmem` (page-directory frame), two `page_table_allocator` closures
72. (`link_user_pages`, `alloc_upages`), and `alloc_kpage`.
73. - Callers assume (Ok): a `KernelFrame` owning one freshly allocated physical
74.   frame that no one else holds. They immediately `clear()` it, wrap it in a
75.   `KernelPage`, or build a page table on it. Ownership/Drop semantics matter:
76.   dropping the returned frame must free it.
77. - Callers assume (Err): nothing was allocated and no frame leaked (the impl
78.   frees the frame if `KernelFrame::new` fails); error is simply propagated with
79.   `?`. **No watermark involvement** — kernel allocation must succeed whenever a
80.   physical frame is available, even below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`.
81. - Callers don't care about: the exact physical address chosen, or the
82.   `frame::alloc` + wrap mechanics.
83. 
84. ### `alloc_many_kernel_frames(&mut self, count, &mut Vec<KernelFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
85. Single caller: `alloc_kpages`. Caller pre-checks the vector is empty and has
86. capacity ≥ `count`, then optionally `clear()`s each frame; on a later clear
87. failure it `clear()`s the whole vec to free everything.
88. - Callers assume (Ok): exactly `count` frames are pushed, and they are
89.   **physically contiguous** (the documented reason: identity-mapped kernel
90.   stacks). Each entry is an owning `KernelFrame`.
91. - Callers assume (Err): the vector is left empty (the impl `clear()`s it and
92.   frees any un-wrapped frames from the contiguous run); nothing leaks. Watermark
93.   is bypassed.
94. - Callers don't care about: how contiguity is obtained
95.   (`frame::alloc_contiguous`) or the base-address arithmetic.
96. - Precondition relied upon by the impl (and satisfied by the caller): `frames`
97.   empty and `capacity ≥ count`.
98. 
99. ### `alloc_many_user_frames(&mut self, count, &mut Vec<UserFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
100. Single caller: `alloc_upages` (L611). Caller defensively `uframes.clear()`s on
101. error, then drains the vec to map each frame.
102. - Callers assume (Ok): exactly `count` `UserFrame`s pushed; **not** required to
103.   be contiguous (they are mapped individually at successive virtual addresses).
104. - Callers assume (Err): `uframes` is emptied (impl `clear()`s on per-frame
105.   failure); request is **watermark-gated** — it is rejected with `OutOfMemory`
106.   if fulfilling it would drop free frames below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. This is the
107.   central guarantee distinguishing user from kernel allocation.
108. - Callers don't care about: pool internals (`Upool::alloc`) or which frames are
109.   handed out.
110. - Precondition relied upon: `frames` empty and `capacity ≥ count`.
111. 
112. ### `alloc_user_frame(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
113. Single caller: CoW page-fault resolution in `vmem.rs:879`. The frame is filled
114. via `memcpy`, installed into a PTE, then `leak()`ed (ownership transferred to the
115. page table).
116. - Callers assume (Ok): one `UserFrame` with a valid `address()`, subject to the
117.   **same watermark check** as `alloc_many_user_frames` (count = 1). Must be a
118.   fast path with no intermediate `Vec`.
119. - Callers assume (Err): nothing allocated; propagated with `?`. On the hot CoW
120.   path, `OutOfMemory` from the watermark is the expected rejection.
121. - Callers don't care about: the watermark threshold value itself, only that the
122.   single-frame path enforces it identically to the bulk path.
123. 
124. ### `check_user_watermark(count)` (private)
125. No external callers. It is the shared gate for the two user-allocation paths and
126. encodes the invariant "after any user allocation, at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK`
127. frames remain free for the kernel." Relevant to the View as the predicate behind
128. the user-vs-kernel asymmetry; not part of the public contract.
129. 
130. ## Abstract Resource
131. `PhysMemoryManager` is the singleton broker over the pool of physical page
132. frames. It hands out **typed, owning frame handles**: `KernelFrame`s (drawn
133. straight from the frame allocator, contiguous on request, never watermark-gated)
134. and `UserFrame`s (drawn from the user `Upool` and gated by a kernel watermark so
135. the kernel always retains `KERNEL_WATERMARK` free frames). Callers observe a
136. partition of frames into allocated/free with per-frame refcounts (the existing
137. `FrameAllocView`), plus a liveness flag that the singleton is initialized
138. (`manager_ready` / `live()`), and never touch the underlying storage mechanisms.
139. 
140. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
141. - **Init-before-use**: every alloc path runs only after `init` succeeded; until
142.   then `get_mut` panics. Callers rely on the subsystem being `live()`.
143. - **Kernel allocations bypass the watermark**; **user allocations are
144.   watermark-gated** and rejected (`OutOfMemory`) when they would drop free frames
145.   below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. `alloc_user_frame` and `alloc_many_user_frames`
146.   enforce this identically (via `check_user_watermark`).
147. - **All-or-nothing bulk allocation**: on success the caller's vector holds
148.   exactly `count` owning handles (contiguous for kernel frames); on failure the
149.   vector is emptied and no frame leaks.
150. - **No leak on failure**: every error path frees frames already taken from the
151.   allocator (kernel wrap-failure free, contiguous-range cleanup, user-pool
152.   `clear`).
153. - **Ownership/Drop discipline**: returned `KernelFrame`/`UserFrame` own their
154.   physical frame; dropping frees it, `leak()` transfers ownership. Callers manage
155.   frame lifetime entirely through these handles.
156. - **Caller-supplied storage contract**: bulk APIs require the passed `Vec` to be
157.   empty with `capacity ≥ count`; otherwise `InvalidArgument`.
158. 
159. ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
160. - Source: added during verification of the enclosing `mm::phys` module
161.   (`mod.rs` / `mod.spec.rs`).
162. - View type: exists — `PhysModView` with field `frames: FrameAllocView`, plus
163.   `initialized` and `manager_ready` flags; accessed via `phys_view()`. The
164.   manager-specific spec file `manager.spec.rs` is currently an empty `verus!{}`
165.   block (no per-function specs yet).
166. - Functions WITH specs touching the manager: only `init` participates indirectly
167.   — `mm/phys/mod.rs::init` ensures `phys_view().live()` after calling
168.   `PhysMemoryManager::init` + `lemma_manager_ready()`. `PhysMemoryManager::init`
169.   itself is `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` (no requires/ensures of its own).
170. - Functions WITHOUT specs: `alloc_kernel_frame`, `alloc_many_kernel_frames`,
171.   `alloc_many_user_frames`, `alloc_user_frame`, `check_user_watermark` — none
172.   carry `verus_spec` yet.
173. 
174. ### Assessment
175. - Coverage: partial. The upstream work modeled subsystem *liveness*
176.   (`initialized` / `manager_ready` / `frames.wf()`) and reservation vocabulary on
177.   `FrameAllocView`, which is what `phys::init` needed. It did **not** specify the
178.   allocation operations.
179. - Strength: weak for this module's purpose. There is no spec expressing the
180.   watermark gate, the allocated/free refcount transitions per alloc, contiguity
181.   for kernel ranges, or the all-or-nothing/no-leak error behavior callers rely
182.   on. `PhysMemoryManager::init` being `external_body` with no ensures means the
183.   `manager_ready` transition is currently asserted only via `lemma_manager_ready`.
184. - View design: the existing `FrameAllocView` (allocated/free sets + refcounts) is
185.   caller-abstract and is the right basis for the alloc specs — it already exposes
186.   exactly what callers observe (which frames are taken, refcounts for CoW).
187.   Remaining work is to write per-function ensures over `phys_view().frames` for
188.   the six target functions; do **not** modify `FrameAllocView`, `Inner`,
189.   `frame_addr_of`, `byte_at_address`, or the `View for Inner` impl.

 See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-manager/find_callers_output.md`
 (generated by `scripts/find_callers_lsp.py`, rust-analyzer LSP, intra-crate).
 
 ## Module Summary
 
 | Category | Count |
 |----------|------:|
 | Total exec functions | 7 |
 | Public / `pub(super)` | 6 |
 | Private | 1 (`check_user_watermark`) |
 | Types | 1 (`PhysMemoryManager`) |
 
 All callers are inside the `kernel` crate. No external crate depends on this
 module, so the entire caller set is the table below.
 
 ## Verification-order Target Functions — call sites
 
 | Function | Visibility | External callers | Where |
 |----------|-----------|-----------------:|-------|
 | `init` | `pub(super)` | 1 | `mm/phys/mod.rs:189` (subsystem `init`) |
 | `alloc_kernel_frame` | `pub` | 4 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:217, 267, 600, 705` |
 | `alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:748` (`alloc_kpages`) |
 | `alloc_many_user_frames` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/manager.rs:611` (`alloc_upages`) |
 | `alloc_user_frame` | `pub` | 1 | `mm/virt/vmem.rs:879` (CoW fault resolve) |
 | `check_user_watermark` | private | 0 external | called by `alloc_many_user_frames` (L177) and `alloc_user_frame` (L205) |
 
 Supporting (not a target, but every alloc reaches the manager through it):
 `get_mut` (`pub unsafe`) — 7 call sites. Every caller obtains the singleton via
 `unsafe { PhysMemoryManager::get_mut() }.<alloc>()`, justified by the kernel being
 single-threaded with interrupts disabled.
 
 ## Trait Obligations
 None. `PhysMemoryManager` implements no traits relevant to dispatch
 (`Drop`/`GlobalAlloc`/`Iterator` etc.). All usage is direct method calls on the
 singleton. The frame ownership wrappers it returns (`KernelFrame`, `UserFrame`)
 *do* carry `Drop` semantics (dropping frees the frame), and callers depend on
 that — see below.
 
 ## Internal Call Graph
 - `alloc_many_user_frames` → `check_user_watermark(count)` → `frame::free_count`,
   `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK`, then `self.upool.alloc()` per frame.
 - `alloc_user_frame` → `check_user_watermark(1)` → `self.upool.alloc()`.
 - `alloc_kernel_frame` → `frame::alloc` → `KernelFrame::new` (frees the frame on
   wrap failure).
 - `alloc_many_kernel_frames` → `frame::alloc_contiguous(count)` →
   `KernelFrame::new` per frame (frees the leftover contiguous range on failure).
 
 Key structural fact for the View: **user** allocations flow through `Upool`
 (`self.upool`) and are watermark-gated; **kernel** allocations go straight to the
 `frame` allocator and bypass the watermark.
 
 ## Caller Expectations
 
 ### `init(upool) -> Result<(), Error>`
 Single caller: `mm/phys/mod.rs::init`, exactly once during single-threaded boot,
 immediately after `Upool::new()`. Followed by `proof!{ lemma_manager_ready(); }`.
 - Callers assume (Ok): the manager singleton now exists and holds the provided
   `upool`; subsequent `get_mut()` will not panic; the subsystem reaches the
   `manager_ready` / `live()` state. This is the post-state the surrounding
   `phys::init` spec advertises (`phys_view().live()`).
 - Callers assume (Err): only `InvalidArgument`, and only on double-init; boot
   treats this as fatal (propagated with `?`).
 - Callers don't care about: the `MaybeUninit` storage, the `AtomicBool` init
   flag, or the atomic ordering. They care only that "after Ok, the manager is
   ready and frame guarantees become meaningful."
 
 ### `alloc_kernel_frame(&mut self) -> Result<KernelFrame, Error>`
 Callers: `new_vmem` (page-directory frame), two `page_table_allocator` closures
 (`link_user_pages`, `alloc_upages`), and `alloc_kpage`.
 - Callers assume (Ok): a `KernelFrame` owning one freshly allocated physical
   frame that no one else holds. They immediately `clear()` it, wrap it in a
   `KernelPage`, or build a page table on it. Ownership/Drop semantics matter:
   dropping the returned frame must free it.
 - Callers assume (Err): nothing was allocated and no frame leaked (the impl
   frees the frame if `KernelFrame::new` fails); error is simply propagated with
   `?`. **No watermark involvement** — kernel allocation must succeed whenever a
   physical frame is available, even below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`.
 - Callers don't care about: the exact physical address chosen, or the
   `frame::alloc` + wrap mechanics.
 
 ### `alloc_many_kernel_frames(&mut self, count, &mut Vec<KernelFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
 Single caller: `alloc_kpages`. Caller pre-checks the vector is empty and has
 capacity ≥ `count`, then optionally `clear()`s each frame; on a later clear
 failure it `clear()`s the whole vec to free everything.
 - Callers assume (Ok): exactly `count` frames are pushed, and they are
   **physically contiguous** (the documented reason: identity-mapped kernel
   stacks). Each entry is an owning `KernelFrame`.
 - Callers assume (Err): the vector is left empty (the impl `clear()`s it and
   frees any un-wrapped frames from the contiguous run); nothing leaks. Watermark
   is bypassed.
 - Callers don't care about: how contiguity is obtained
   (`frame::alloc_contiguous`) or the base-address arithmetic.
 - Precondition relied upon by the impl (and satisfied by the caller): `frames`
   empty and `capacity ≥ count`.
 
 ### `alloc_many_user_frames(&mut self, count, &mut Vec<UserFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
 Single caller: `alloc_upages` (L611). Caller defensively `uframes.clear()`s on
 error, then drains the vec to map each frame.
 - Callers assume (Ok): exactly `count` `UserFrame`s pushed; **not** required to
   be contiguous (they are mapped individually at successive virtual addresses).
 - Callers assume (Err): `uframes` is emptied (impl `clear()`s on per-frame
   failure); request is **watermark-gated** — it is rejected with `OutOfMemory`
   if fulfilling it would drop free frames below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. This is the
   central guarantee distinguishing user from kernel allocation.
 - Callers don't care about: pool internals (`Upool::alloc`) or which frames are
   handed out.
 - Precondition relied upon: `frames` empty and `capacity ≥ count`.
 
 ### `alloc_user_frame(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error>`
 Single caller: CoW page-fault resolution in `vmem.rs:879`. The frame is filled
 via `memcpy`, installed into a PTE, then `leak()`ed (ownership transferred to the
 page table).
 - Callers assume (Ok): one `UserFrame` with a valid `address()`, subject to the
   **same watermark check** as `alloc_many_user_frames` (count = 1). Must be a
   fast path with no intermediate `Vec`.
 - Callers assume (Err): nothing allocated; propagated with `?`. On the hot CoW
   path, `OutOfMemory` from the watermark is the expected rejection.
 - Callers don't care about: the watermark threshold value itself, only that the
   single-frame path enforces it identically to the bulk path.
 
 ### `check_user_watermark(count)` (private)
 No external callers. It is the shared gate for the two user-allocation paths and
 encodes the invariant "after any user allocation, at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK`
 frames remain free for the kernel." Relevant to the View as the predicate behind
 the user-vs-kernel asymmetry; not part of the public contract.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 `PhysMemoryManager` is the singleton broker over the pool of physical page
 frames. It hands out **typed, owning frame handles**: `KernelFrame`s (drawn
 straight from the frame allocator, contiguous on request, never watermark-gated)
 and `UserFrame`s (drawn from the user `Upool` and gated by a kernel watermark so
 the kernel always retains `KERNEL_WATERMARK` free frames). Callers observe a
 partition of frames into allocated/free with per-frame refcounts (the existing
 `FrameAllocView`), plus a liveness flag that the singleton is initialized
 (`manager_ready` / `live()`), and never touch the underlying storage mechanisms.
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 - **Init-before-use**: every alloc path runs only after `init` succeeded; until
   then `get_mut` panics. Callers rely on the subsystem being `live()`.
 - **Kernel allocations bypass the watermark**; **user allocations are
   watermark-gated** and rejected (`OutOfMemory`) when they would drop free frames
   below `KERNEL_WATERMARK`. `alloc_user_frame` and `alloc_many_user_frames`
   enforce this identically (via `check_user_watermark`).
 - **All-or-nothing bulk allocation**: on success the caller's vector holds
   exactly `count` owning handles (contiguous for kernel frames); on failure the
   vector is emptied and no frame leaks.
 - **No leak on failure**: every error path frees frames already taken from the
   allocator (kernel wrap-failure free, contiguous-range cleanup, user-pool
   `clear`).
 - **Ownership/Drop discipline**: returned `KernelFrame`/`UserFrame` own their
   physical frame; dropping frees it, `leak()` transfers ownership. Callers manage
   frame lifetime entirely through these handles.
 - **Caller-supplied storage contract**: bulk APIs require the passed `Vec` to be
   empty with `capacity ≥ count`; otherwise `InvalidArgument`.
 
 ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
 - Source: added during verification of the enclosing `mm::phys` module
   (`mod.rs` / `mod.spec.rs`).
 - View type: exists — `PhysModView` with field `frames: FrameAllocView`, plus
   `initialized` and `manager_ready` flags; accessed via `phys_view()`. The
   manager-specific spec file `manager.spec.rs` is currently an empty `verus!{}`
   block (no per-function specs yet).
 - Functions WITH specs touching the manager: only `init` participates indirectly
   — `mm/phys/mod.rs::init` ensures `phys_view().live()` after calling
   `PhysMemoryManager::init` + `lemma_manager_ready()`. `PhysMemoryManager::init`
   itself is `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` (no requires/ensures of its own).
 - Functions WITHOUT specs: `alloc_kernel_frame`, `alloc_many_kernel_frames`,
   `alloc_many_user_frames`, `alloc_user_frame`, `check_user_watermark` — none
   carry `verus_spec` yet.
 
 ### Assessment
 - Coverage: partial. The upstream work modeled subsystem *liveness*
   (`initialized` / `manager_ready` / `frames.wf()`) and reservation vocabulary on
   `FrameAllocView`, which is what `phys::init` needed. It did **not** specify the
   allocation operations.
 - Strength: weak for this module's purpose. There is no spec expressing the
   watermark gate, the allocated/free refcount transitions per alloc, contiguity
   for kernel ranges, or the all-or-nothing/no-leak error behavior callers rely
   on. `PhysMemoryManager::init` being `external_body` with no ensures means the
   `manager_ready` transition is currently asserted only via `lemma_manager_ready`.
 - View design: the existing `FrameAllocView` (allocated/free sets + refcounts) is
   caller-abstract and is the right basis for the alloc specs — it already exposes
   exactly what callers observe (which frames are taken, refcounts for CoW).
   Remaining work is to write per-function ensures over `phys_view().frames` for
   the six target functions; do **not** modify `FrameAllocView`, `Inner`,
   `frame_addr_of`, `byte_at_address`, or the `View for Inner` impl.

3. description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
4. ---
5. 
6. # AST Consistency Check
7. 
8. Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
9. for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.
10. 
11. ## Tools
12. 
13. The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
14. ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.
15. 
16. `scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
17. - `count` — quick pass/fail
18. - `summary` — per-element status table
19. - `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
20. - `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs
21. 
22. The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
23. from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:
24. 
25. ```bash
26. # Explicit original file:
27. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count
28. 
29. # Via git ref:
30. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count
31. 
32. # Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
33. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
34. ```
35. 
36. `diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.
37. 
38. **MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
39. functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
40. `ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.
41. 
42. ## Pre-Approved Deviations
43. 
44. These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
45. process needed, but still document with a comment:
46. 
47. | Original | Verus Version | Reason |
48. |----------|--------------|--------|
49. | `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
50. | `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
51. | `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
52. | `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
53. | `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
54. | `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
55. | `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
56. | `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |
57. 
58. ### Bug Fix Deviations
59. 
60. Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
61. - Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
62. - Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
63. - Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
64. - Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
65.   bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill
66. 
67. ## Handling MISMATCHes
68. 
69. When the checker reports a MISMATCH:
70. 
71. 1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
72.    `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
73.    manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
74.    Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
75. 2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
76.    keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
77. 3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
78.    change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
79.    - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
80.    - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
81.    - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
82. 4. **If confirmed, document with full evidence.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
83.    comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
84.    what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.
85.

 | `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |

   bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill

 When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

    `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
    manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
